title: Friday Night Database Recovery Crash Course (A True Story)
description:
A story about database backups and restore drills, Point-In-Time Recovery with the Write-Ahead Log, RPO and RTO, alert fatigue, and incident response.

This video is built for learning! To keep things clear, some details have been oversimplified.

segments.text: Friday Night Wojak is trying to fix this storage issue on production database, but instead he ends up deleting the entire thing and they don't have a backup.
I mean, a backup job runs every night, but somehow there's still no backup.
Now, there are multiple lessons in this story.
Any of them could have changed how things ended for Wojak.
I know this because I've been running different types of databases in production for years now at companies of all sizes, and I've deleted the production database myself.
So everything you see in this video is based on a real experience with real tools along the way.
We'll cover the mistake that led to this and what could have saved everyone's weekend. But first, let's go back a few hours.
It all started on a Friday afternoon. It was almost 6 p.m.
and everyone was leaving the office to start the weekend except Wojak.
He was sitting there staring at the screen, looking at this SQL statement he was about to run on production database.
He got hired at this startup three months ago as a junior backend engineer.
It was another one of those AI driven customer support slash lead generation of startups.
It took Wojak seven months of sending resumes every single day to land this position.
So in his mind, he could not afford to lose this opportunity.
And for these three months, he's been using AI coding tools heavily, and it worked pretty well for him.
He deliver more tasks than anyone else on the team, and that gave him a lot of confidence, maybe a bit too much. That morning he ran into Mr.
CEO in the elevator. Wojak, right.
I've heard a lot of good things about you.
Hey, I saw this post on LinkedIn the other day.
Apparently, if we get ISO certified investors take you way more seriously.
The thing is, to get certified, you need a record of every change that happens in your database.
It's not urgent, but you think you could make that happen.
Now, it didn't take Wojak a long time to come up with a SQL statement for this.
Or rather, he just asked ChatGPT how to keep track of every query that runs against a PostgreSQL database.
The simplest way is to enable statement logging, set the log statement to all and reload the config. He tested this exact
statement on the test environment on a test database almost identical to the one running on the production, and it was working.
So he connected to the production database, pasted the same two lines, and sat there with his finger on the Enter key. Wojak... Wojak!
It's already 6 p.m.. Aren't you leaving? Yeah, I was about to leave. Just finishing my task.
Bro, you're making the rest of us look bad by doing so many tasks. Take it easy on yourself. Burnout is a real thing.
The only thing Wojak is thinking about right now is finishing this task today.
So on Monday, he can walk up to the CEO and say, done this query.
Just add more verbosity to the logs, he thinks.
Besides, I already tested this on the staging, so. Must be safe.
For about 4.5 hours later, Wojak received this alert from the production alerts channel in a slack critical production database.
Volume is running out of his space.
Current usage is at 91% and the action required section.
He sees this line check for huge log files. He also sees the graph.
Disk usage has been slowly increasing for weeks and sat around 77%.
And then at 6:01 p.m., a sharp increase is straight up to 91%.
You see, their production PostgreSQL database is not on a managed service like AWS. RDS. It's self-hosted.
It runs on their own servers inside the Kubernetes cluster right alongside the application itself. Actually, they used to be on RDS.
About a year ago.
They migrated to this self-managed Postgres to save money.
Remember that they created a 250 gigabyte the storage volume, and connected this storage space to the database pod
under the slash mnt slash database volume address.
They also configured Postgres to store both the data and the logs on the same volume.
Now think about what Wojak did four hours ago.
He set the log statement to all, which means from that moment on, Postgres writes every single SQL statement.
It executes is straight to that log directory. And this is production. There's a lot of traffic. So the volume is started filling up fast.
Back to Wojak.
He takes the screenshot of this alert, pasted into ChatGPT and asked, what should I do? ChatGPT says to treat this as urgent.
First find out what is consuming this space and gives him a disk usage command.
So Wojak attaches a terminal to the production pod and runs the disk usage command. 189GB in the data directory, 38GB in the logs directory.
He passes the result back to ChatGPT. The log files are safe to delete.
Postgres doesn't need them to run delete them to free up a space.
Now Wojak has zero experience maintaining a production database, but right now he's not thinking about that. He's thinking about his reputation.
He made a mistake. He doesn't want anyone to know.
If I fix this quickly, he thinks nobody will find out. So he start pasting the commands. One by one.
He set the log directory variable, verifies this point to the right directory, and lists the log files.
Then he goes back to ChatGPT to copy the final command The remove command.
But while he's doing that his sessions times out error lost connection to pod.
He attaches to the pod again gets a fresh shell session and paste the command he already copied.
RM rf log directory slash star and presses. Enter. The command hangs for a second. Good.
He thinks it's working, but then he starts seeing errors. Cannot remove dev. mqueue cannot remove etc hostname.
He doesn't understand why this command.
Trying to remove files under dev or under etc paths. So he does what he always does.
He copies the error and paste them into ChatGPT.
ChatGPT starts quote unquote reasoning and shortly after responds Stop the command. Right now press Ctrl c in the terminal.
Immediately you see he saved the log folder path in a temporary variable, the log directory variable.
When his first terminal session timed out, the temporary variable was wiped in his new terminal session, the log directory was
completely blank, so log directory slash star became a slash a star,
which means deleting everything from the root directory up. His soul left his body.
He jumps back to the terminal and smashes control. C harder than he ever did in his life. The command stops. He types ls ls command not found.
Even ls is gone. He effectively nuked the database. It's 10:45 p.m. now.
He receives a wave of alerts on his slack. Database is down. Application is down. Health checks are failing.
And then people start posting in the general channel. Is the app down for anyone else? Customers are emailing us at 10:49.
He goes to the developers channel, mentions everyone and writes we have a production incident.
He creates a Google meet, paste the link in the thread and joins the call.
Now here's the first mistake in the incident response itself.
People in the general are asking what's going on and nobody's answering them.
Communication is one of the first principle of the incident response.
You keep the rest of the company and your customers updated about the status at all time.
Even if this status is, we don't know yet. Silence is the worst. Update 20 minutes pass and nobody joins. At 11:09.
He calls Zoomer the DevOps engineer and George the tech lead.
Shortly after, they both join Wojak. What happened?
I might have accidentally deleted the entire production database. You did what?
I deleted the root directory of the production database, and.
He proceeded to explain exactly how it happened. It's 11:13 p.m..
Production has been down for 28 minutes after short back and forth they split the work.
George takes care of communication and Zoomer restore the database from this morning's backup. Now. Luckily they do have backups.
Every morning at 4 a.m., an automated job copies the entire database into a single backup file and uploads it to a S3 bucket on AWS.
But here's the thing the backup was taken at 4 a.m.
on Friday, and the incident happened at 10:45 p.m., so all the Friday data is gone and they could have avoided that.
You see, before Postgres changes any data on the disk, it first record what it's about to do in a running diary.
called the Write ahead Log.
If Postgres crashes, it reads this diary and re-applies the changes to recover.
Now imagine if you save a copy of this write ahead log files somewhere safe, like an S3 bucket. Then you have a recovery method.
Way better than just daily database dumps. It called a point in time recovery. You take your last full backup.
You replay the write ahead log on top of it, and you tell it to stop, say, at 10:43 p.m., one minute before the data was deleted.
On a managed service like RDS.
There is essentially a single checkbox to enable point in time recovery. Now back to Zoomer.
Zoomer is fairly new in his DevOps role too, and right now he's searching in Notion for a database recovery guideline because he's not sure
which S3 bucket the backups are in, or how to even start a restore.
The only page he finds was updated a year ago, and it's about restoring the backup on the RDS.
The way the database was set up before completely useless with their self-hosted Postgres now.
So now he has to dig through the S3 buckets in the AWS console, hoping to recognize the right one by its name.
He also needs to piece together a restore procedure by googling and asking ChatGPT.
So lesson number one no matter where you work and what's the size of your company, you need to have a database backup and restore
procedure document that clearly explains a step by step.
How are backups are created and how do you restore them.
But that document alone is not enough yet.
Backup is only a backup if you test that restoring it.
So you need to run restore drills, say at least once a year.
During the drill, you restore a fresh database from your backup, following your documentation, and make sure everything works.
You also want to keep track of two numbers. RPO and RTO. RPO is the recovery point.
Objective It's the maximum amount of data loss you can tolerate measured in time.
For example, taking a daily backup at 4 a.m. means an RPO of up to 24 hours. RTO is a recovery time objective.
It's how long your system can be down before it's severely damaged the business. Now, these are business decisions.
So you agree on these targets with the management of your company, and then you design your backups around them.
Meanwhile, back on the call, it seemed like Zoomer found a backup bucket. But there is a problem. I can't find today's backup.
Actually, the latest backup I see here is from 12 days ago. Try changing the sort order. No, nothing.
They refused to believe it, but unfortunately, it's true. Here's what happened.
The database was growing all the time, and the backup job had a timeout of 30 minutes.
12 days ago, the database got big enough that the backup job couldn't finish in 30 minutes. So Kubernetes killed the job.
And the same thing happened every day after that.
Now they're getting alerts about this every day in the dev alerts channel in a slack warning job production Postgres backup failed.
Reason deadline exceeded.
But the channel gets hundreds of other alerts every day as well.
Most of those alerts are either not configured properly or they shouldn't exist in the first place.
So one alert that actually mattered scrolled by 12 days in a row and no one reacted to it. This is called alert fatigue.
It happens when you receive so many alerts that you stop paying attention to any of them.
Your brain get conditioned that a red icon in the slack means nothing, because the last 100 red icons meant nothing.
So here's the rule every alert should be actionable if no immediate action is expected.
When it's fires, either delete it or turn it into a dashboard. It's almost midnight.
The only option left is restoring the backup from 12 days ago, which means all customer data leads, and activity from the past 12 days is gone.
Before we do this, I need to call Mr. CEO and tell him what we're. About to do. Five minutes later, Mr. CEO joins the call.
What happened here?
They explain everything and then complete silence. Nobody says a word. All the hope is lost. Only a miracle can save their weekend.
And suddenly Mr. CEO breaks the silence. Don't worry, kids, I have a backup.
He reaches into his back pocket and pulls out a USB drive. It says please subscribe. Except that didn't happen. What actually happened is Mr.
CEO asked the worst question one can ask in this situation. Who's responsible for this?
Whoa, Jack, didn't I say this wasn't urgent? Why did you do this? Why?
And right before he leaves the call, he says I. Want all of the data back now. I don't care how. It's 12:15 a.m..
Everyone is exhausted and stressed after a few minutes of discussion, they come up with a plan, restore the backup from 12 days ago,
then try to fill the missing data gaps from the other sources.
For example, pull user accounts and emails from Google Analytics, fetch subscription details from Stripe, and so on. They know they won't recover everything.
Messages, leads.
Most of it is lost for good, and they know they'll spend the entire weekend writing custom scripts to stitch the data together.
But at this point, there is no other option. So Zoomer restarts the database pod.
This is now a brand new, completely empty database.
Then he attaches the terminal and tries to pull the old backup from S3.
And needless to say, he's following instructions from ChatGPT and he ran into one problem after another.
The database container doesn't even have a tool installed to download files from S3.
Then he realizes the backup bucket is private and the database pod has no access to it. So he has two options. Do it properly.
Create a IAM role that grants the pod access to the bucket, or do it in a dirty, quick way. Make the bucket public.
Pull the backup file and make it private again afterwards.
Which, by the way, opens a security hole for the company.
If he forgets to make it private again and again. This is exactly why you prepare for this.
Because when you're in an incident with all of that stress and pressure, it's so easy to make a mistake, and each mistakes cascade into the next one and make the situation worse.
They spend the next three hours until 3 a.m. trying to restore what they can. Zoomer is exhausted.
He can't focus, and he keep making mistakes, which makes everything take even longer. Here's another lesson.
If you're in a long running incident like this one, you need a team members who can rotate shifts.
One person actively working on recovery while the others rest. A tired engineer is a dangerous engineer, so they decide to end the call, get some sleep, and rejoin at 6 a.m.
with more backend and data engineers.
